newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jobless claims fell last week, surprising markets.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobless claims fell last week, surprising markets.

text.p: New applications for unemployment benefits fell by an unexpectedly sharp 15,000 last week, the Labour Department said Thursday, ending four straight weeks of rises.
"Most of us were expecting something flat so this was a surprise," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany. "It hints that tomorrow's employment numbers will be strong."
The government issues its August jobs report Friday.

The larger-than-forecast decline in jobless claims sent the inflation-sensitive U.S. Treasury market skidding, with the benchmark 30-year bond off half a point. Its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, climbed to 7.15 percent from 7.10 percent late Wednesday as traders anticipated a strong August jobs report.
New filings for jobless benefits fell to 316,000 in the week ended Aug. 31 from 331,000 in the prior week, the department said. Wall Street economists had forecast initial claims at 335,000.

The four-week moving average, which levels out the often-volatile weekly figures, totalled 323,500, up 500 from the previous week's 323,000. The average is considered a more accurate measurement of employment trends than the weekly figure.
Benefit rolls rose 8,000 to reach 2.525 million in the week ended Aug. 24, the latest period for which figures were available. That was up from 2.517 million the prior week, the department said.
One state reported an increase of more than 1,000 in initial claims on an unadjusted basis in the week ended Aug. 24, the latest for which the data are available, Labour said.
Tennessee, with 1,061 new claims, cited layoffs in the food, textile, apparel, glass and electronic equipment industries.
Four states reported decreases in initial claims exceeding 1,000, in the Aug. 24 week, the department said.
They were California, with 1,627 fewer claims, Delaware, with 1,564, Michigan, with 1,350 and Ohio, with 1,006.
Delaware reported fewer layoffs in the automobile industry. California, Michigan and Ohio had no comment.
